definition: A theoretical result stating that a neural network with at least one hidden layer and a sufficient number of neurons can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy.
details: The universal approximation theorem provides theoretical justification for why neural networks are such flexible function approximators, though it says nothing about how easy such functions are to actually learn via gradient-based training.

explainer.lead: The universal approximation theorem states that a neural network with at least one hidden layer and enough neurons can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy. It matters as theoretical justification for why neural networks are such flexible function approximators.

tiers.eli5: Given enough knobs and dials, a network can mimic any smooth curve you draw, no matter how wiggly.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers cite it to justify using sufficiently wide or deep networks for function fitting, but must remember it says nothing about how easily such functions are learned by gradient-based training. The pitfall is treating the guarantee of representability as a guarantee of trainability or generalization.
tiers.paperLevel: A theoretical result: a network with at least one hidden layer and a sufficient number of neurons can approximate any continuous function to arbitrary accuracy; it makes no claim about ease of learning via gradient-based training.

explainer.example: A single-hidden-layer network with enough neurons can approximate a continuous target function to within any chosen error tolerance.
